title: The Mystery of the Missing Ribbons
markdown:
Misty Kettle was a place where evening made the air soft and quiet, as if the world held its breath. The most wonderful sight was the string of lanterns along the village path, each with a pretty ribbon that fluttered like a sleepy butterfly. Then one twilight, the ribbons started to disappear.

Eira was an elf whose hair shimmered like moonlight. She smoothed her tunic, linen rustling. She loved puzzles. The missing ribbons tickled her curiosity like a feather. Beside her, Flicker, a tiny dragon with sunset scales—orange, pink, purple—puffed marshmallow smoke, his happy sign. “Ribbons gone, Eira?” Happy squeaks and trills.

“That’s a funny thing about ribbons, Flicker. They don’t fly away by themselves. Especially not all at once.”

They set out. The sun had set behind jagged peaks: purple, rose, streaks of orange. Cool air, damp moss after light rain. Far away, sheep bleating toward sleep. Eira, eager, almost tripped. A circle of mushrooms stacked neatly, a little tower, plump speckled caps. “That’s odd. Mushrooms don’t stack themselves. They’re not very ambitious.”

Flicker nudged the lowest. It wobbled. “Maybe a naughty badger?” Tail twitch.

“Maybe.” She looked down the darkening path. Lanterns without their usual glow. A flutter in her tummy: excitement, a little worry. The villagers would feel gloomy, like a cloudy day, if the path stayed bare. They had to find the ribbons before night took the last of the light.

Deeper into whispering woods. Tall trees like silent giants. A soft pop, then a frustrated sigh. Behind a mossy boulder: a young wizard named Elmsworth, robes messy, pointy hat tilted over one eye, a long silvery wand, a cloud of shimmering dust drifting from it like ribbons on a breeze.

He mumbled. “Not bright enough. More floaty. And where has my—oh dear. Oh, my goodness gracious.”

Eira stepped forward. “Excuse me, sir? Are you perhaps looking for some ribbons?”

He jumped. “Goodness gracious! An elf. And a dragonling. Yes, I suppose I am. I was trying a new spell to make the lanterns extra bright. Instead of light, I seem to have made thin ribbons. If I don’t fix this soon, my tutor will be very unhappy. He expects me to have mastered it by sunrise.”

The dust swirled, catching moonlight like tiny diamonds. Flicker sneezed a tiny fizzing spark. Eira’s mind put pieces together. “The mushrooms. Did you stack them?”

“Why, yes. Extra magical support. The spell needs exact energy. The earth seemed a good place to anchor it. Just for a moment.”

He had been so focused on spectacular that he forgot how the spell got there. It was not making ribbons from nothing. It was unravelling them from wherever it could, tying them to mushroom towers as temporary anchors. A gust, a wrongness, and they had been released into his dusty cloud.

The floating strands were beautiful. Flicker, worry forgotten, chased one, batting with a playful paw, sunset scales flashing. But the village lanterns were dark. Children would be waiting for the familiar glow. The path would feel lonely.

Elmsworth’s shoulders slumped. “It’s no use. I’ll have to give up. My tutor will think I’m a terrible wizard. Maybe I’m just not good at this.” The proud look faded, showing a boy trying his best.

“Wait,” Eira said, gentle and steady. “Perhaps you don’t have to. Perhaps we can fix it. Together.” Flicker was trying to wear a floating ribbon like a scarf. “Flicker can help gather them. I think I know how to help your spell work properly, so it doesn’t borrow things it shouldn’t.”

Hope flickered. “You do? How?”

“Your spell wants to tie things. If we give it the right kind of things, and show it exactly where, it might work. And we can give back what it borrowed.”

Elmsworth, with her patient explanations, cast a simpler spell. Thin ribbons coaxed toward the mushroom towers where they had first landed. Flicker’s warm breath, like a gentle summer breeze, herded the dancing strands. Eira gathered the now-stable ribbons and tied them. Not a fight. Working together. Then a very gentle spell guiding them back to the lanterns, soft glow returning one by one. For it to hold, Elmsworth used up the last of his experimental magic—the prize he had been so proud of—so the ribbons would not unravel again. He watched them float back, a small almost-wistful smile: sadness for the magic let go, pride for what they had done.

They walked to the village. Lanterns warm, shadows chased. Flicker trotted, scales catching light. Elmsworth calmer, robes tidied, hat straight.

Later, they say, he used the stacked mushrooms as teacups: earthy little saucers that kept tea from spilling. Flicker kept a soft spot for ribbons, sometimes tying one around his tail, wiggling, on evenings when Misty Kettle’s lanterns glowed and the ribbons danced, and nobody needed a lesson spoken aloud.
